draft.exec:
You need a public web application hosted on Alibaba Cloud.

This proposal lays out a standard architecture in Singapore using edge acceleration, compute across two zones, managed database and storage.

The design keeps the app available during zone issues, handles traffic changes without manual work and stores data reliably.

needs.need: A new web app needs reliable hosting that stays online if a server or zone fails.
needs.answer: Compute, load balancing and the database each run in two zones. If one zone has an issue, the other takes over so users stay connected.

needs.need: Traffic to a public web app can change quickly and overwhelm fixed servers.
needs.answer: Auto Scaling adds or removes servers based on load. You pay for extra capacity only when visitors arrive, protecting response times without overbuying.

needs.need: Public apps face slow loads and attacks from the open internet.
needs.answer: Edge Security Acceleration caches content closer to users and blocks common web attacks before they reach your servers, reducing page load time and breach risk.

outcomes.title: Stays online through zone failures
outcomes.text: Servers, the load balancer, cache and database all span two zones. A failure in one zone leaves the other running, keeping the app reachable.

outcomes.title: Costs track actual visitor traffic
outcomes.text: Auto Scaling adjusts server count by load. You avoid paying for idle machines during quiet hours while handling peaks without manual intervention.

outcomes.title: Faster pages for global visitors
outcomes.text: Edge caching serves static files from locations near users. This reduces wait times, which businesses that run web apps usually need to keep visitors engaged.

why.dns: Directs visitors to the correct entry point for your domain. Without it, users cannot resolve your address to reach the app.
why.esa: Speeds up page loads and blocks web attacks at the edge before they hit your servers. Leaving it out exposes the app directly to internet traffic and slower responses.
why.alb: Splits incoming requests across servers in both zones so no single machine takes all the load. Without it, a server failure drops active connections.
why.ecs: Runs your web application code with full operating system control. This is the core compute; without it there is no application to serve.
why.ess: Adds or removes servers automatically as traffic rises or falls. Without it you must guess peak capacity and either overpay or risk slowdowns.
why.tair: Holds user sessions and frequently read data in memory so pages load fast. Without it every request hits the main database, slowing responses under load.
why.rds: Stores application data with a standby copy in another zone. Without managed backups and failover, a database issue risks permanent data loss.
why.oss: Stores uploaded files and media separately from the servers. Keeping large files on compute disks would waste expensive capacity and complicate scaling.
why.sls: Collects logs centrally so your team can find errors quickly. Without it diagnosing outages requires checking each server manually, extending downtime.

tradeoffs.text: The design assumes about 10,000 users and a public audience. Actual traffic patterns may require different instance sizes or scaling rules.
tradeoffs.mitigation: Confirm expected user count and peak times to size the initial fleet correctly.

tradeoffs.text: The type of web app is not yet defined. An e-commerce shop and a SaaS platform have different security and caching needs.
tradeoffs.mitigation: Specify the workload type so we can tune ESA rules and database sizing.

tradeoffs.text: User location is unknown. Edge performance depends on where most visitors connect from.
tradeoffs.mitigation: Confirm if users are mainly in Singapore, Southeast Asia or worldwide.
